title: Muharram: a new year
hook: the Islamic calendar begins from the Hijra, and the new year is quiet reflection
carry: a new year from the hijra

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Block B, the word rasul, and your line was they all said the same one thing. Which prophet did you name as the one you feel close to? Day five hundred two, and a new stretch of the path.
screen: `THEY ALL SAID THE SAME ONE THING.`

segments.voice: On the first night of the Islamic new year, in many Muslim communities, there are no fireworks at midnight. No countdown. Some families exchange greetings, some mosques hold a talk, and for many people it passes quietly, like a page turning. For the next two weeks, this path steps out of the surahs and walks through the Islamic year itself: its holy days, its months, its fasts and feasts. And the first question is simple. Why does this calendar start where it does?

The Islamic calendar counts from the Hijra, the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ emigration from Mecca to Medina, in the year 622 of the common era. That's why it's called Hijri, and why dates are marked AH, after the Hijra. The choice was made years later, under the second caliph, 'Umar. Letters were arriving with months but no years, and people needed a common count. Reports say they considered the Prophet's birth, or the first revelation, and chose the Hijra instead: the moment a persecuted group became a community with a home. The year was set to begin with Muharram, which reports say was already felt as the turn of the year, after the pilgrimage season, even though the journey itself took place a little later in the year. Surah At-Tawbah says: "Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months", and four of them are sacred. Muharram is one of the four. The months are lunar, each beginning with the new crescent moon, and what that does to the holy days is where these two weeks will end. A hadith in Muslim's collection calls Muharram the month of God, and says the best fast after Ramadan is in it. There is no set ritual for the new year itself. Some Muslims use it to remember the turning point the calendar counts from, and to ask where they themselves are heading. For Shia Muslims, the month also opens a season of mourning, which we'll come to in two days.
screen: `COUNTED FROM THE HIJRA, 622.` · `CHOSEN UNDER 'UMAR.` · `TWELVE MONTHS, FOUR SACRED.` · `MONTHS BY THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one intention for the year. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think back over the last twelve months: one thing you're glad of, one thing you'd leave behind. Then choose one intention for the year ahead. Small and real, something you could still be doing next Muharram. Say it to yourself in one sentence. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Hijri. The Islamic calendar, counted from the Hijra, the emigration to Medina: twelve lunar months, beginning with Muharram. Today's word.
Your line: a new year from the hijra. Today, write your one intention down somewhere you'll see it again, a note on your phone or a slip in your wallet. Day five hundred two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims greet one another at the start of Muharram and reflect on the Hijra; there is no prescribed new year ritual, and practice varies widely between communities.
